title: All in a Row: Compressed Convolution Networks for Graphs
authors: Junshu Sun¹², Shuhui Wang¹³, Xinzhe Han¹², Zhe Xue⁴, Qingming Huang¹²³
institutes: ¹Key Laboratory of Intelligent Information Processing, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
²School of Computer Science and Technology, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
⁴Beijing Key Laboratory of Intelligent Telecommunication Software and Multimedia, School of Computer Science, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
title_audio_script: Welcome. This is "All in a Row: Compressed Convolution Networks for Graphs", an ICML 2023 paper from the Institute of Computing Technology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and collaborators. The work asks a simple question: can we run standard, CNN-style Euclidean convolution directly on graphs? The authors answer yes, by learning a differentiable permutation that lines all the graph's nodes up in a row, and then sliding a diagonal convolution kernel across them. The resulting model, called CoCN, learns hierarchical graph representations end to end and sets new state of the art on both node and graph classification benchmarks.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.necessary: Convolutional GNNs built on graph polynomials are weakly expressive under limited parameters and cannot perform hierarchical representation learning without extra node clustering or node-drop pooling.
sections.additional: Euclidean CNNs escape both limits via local feature learning and global parameter sharing, but their convolution cannot be applied to irregular, non-grid graph structures.
sections.audio_script: Convolutional graph neural networks have a pair of stubborn weaknesses. First, because their filters are built from graph polynomials, they are not very expressive when the parameter budget is small. Second, they cannot learn hierarchical, multi-scale representations on their own; they need bolt-on tricks like node clustering or node dropping to extract features at different scales. Ordinary convolutional neural networks, the kind used for images, do not have these problems at all. Thanks to local feature learning and shared filters, they naturally capture diverse, multi-scale patterns. The catch is that their Euclidean convolution assumes regular grid data and simply does not apply to the irregular structure of a graph.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.necessary: Generalizing Euclidean convolution to graphs is hard: convolution is sensitive to spatial order, yet GNNs must stay permutation invariant, and prior graph-regularization methods are decoupled from the convolution and cannot be optimized per task.
sections.additional: Earlier node-sequence-selection schemes produce fixed, less informative regularized graphs because their ordering is independent of the downstream learning objective.
sections.audio_script: So why not just borrow Euclidean convolution for graphs? The difficulty is a fundamental tension. Convolution is sensitive to spatial order, meaning it cares about the arrangement of its inputs. Graph neural networks, by contrast, must be permutation invariant, producing the same answer no matter how the nodes are numbered. Earlier approaches tried to regularize graphs by selecting a node ordering, but that ordering was chosen independently of the convolution that followed, so it could not be tuned for the actual task and often threw away useful information. What is missing is a way to arrange nodes that is both differentiable and learned end to end.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.necessary: The paper introduces a differentiable graph-regularization method that applies learnable permutations to constrain all nodes into a row with permutation invariance, and builds Compressed Convolution Network (CoCN), which applies CNN-style diagonal convolution and pooling for end-to-end hierarchical graph representation learning.
sections.additional: CoCN is validated across node and graph classification benchmarks, beating competitive convolutional GNNs and graph-pooling models while cutting permutation-modeling cost from O(n!) to O(n²).
sections.audio_script: This paper makes two core contributions. The first is a differentiable regularization for graphs: a learnable permutation that constrains all the nodes into a single row while preserving permutation invariance, so that Euclidean convolution can finally be applied to graph data. The second is the model built on top of it, the Compressed Convolution Network, or CoCN. CoCN follows the same local-feature-learning and global-parameter-sharing principles as image CNNs, learns both node features and structure features, and can be trained fully end to end. Across a wide range of node and graph classification benchmarks, it outperforms competitive convolutional GNNs and graph pooling models.

sections.heading: Method
sections.necessary: CoCN has four modules: input, permutation generation, convolution, and output. Permutation generation regresses node positions and converts them into a relaxed, differentiable permutation matrix; diagonal convolution then slides a kernel along the diagonal of the permuted node-feature and edge-feature matrices, while compressed pooling shrinks the structure matrix from the anti-diagonal direction and transposed convolution up-samples for node classification.
sections.additional: Positions are computed with an MLP smoothed by the graph Laplacian so that similar or nearby nodes land in adjacent positions; multiple permutation heads generate diverse arrangements, and the learnable permutation reduces permutation modeling from O(n!) to O(n²), enabling mini-batch training on large graphs.
sections.audio_script: Here is how CoCN works. It has four modules: input, permutation generation, convolution, and output. The permutation generation module first regresses an absolute position for each node, using a multilayer perceptron on node features smoothed by the graph Laplacian, so that connected or similar nodes receive nearby positions. Those positions are turned into a relaxed permutation matrix, a differentiable relaxation controlled by a factor tau that provably converges to a true permutation as tau grows. Once the nodes are permuted into a row, the model applies diagonal convolution: instead of sliding a kernel column by column and then row by row as in image convolution, it slides the kernel along the diagonal of the permuted edge-feature and node-feature matrices, extracting individual node features and the structure between them at the same time. Compressed pooling then squeezes the structure matrix from the anti-diagonal direction to build a hierarchy, and transposed convolution up-samples the features back for node-level predictions. Crucially, learning the permutation this way drops the cost of permutation modeling from n factorial down to n squared, which is what makes the method scale to large graphs.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.necessary: Graph classification uses six TU datasets — MUTAG, PROTEINS, NCI1, IMDB-BINARY, IMDB-MULTI, COLLAB — and node classification uses six heterophilic datasets — Chameleon, Squirrel, Cornell, Texas, Wisconsin, Actor.
sections.additional: The authors additionally evaluate on de-duplicated filtered Chameleon/Squirrel and on three large-scale graphs (questions, amazon-ratings, genius) with mini-batch Cluster-GCN training to test scalability.
sections.audio_script: The evaluation is broad. For graph classification, the authors use six standard datasets: the biochemical graphs MUTAG, PROTEINS, and NCI1, and the social-network graphs COLLAB, IMDB-Binary, and IMDB-Multi, all under ten-fold cross-validation. For node classification, they use six heterophilic benchmarks: Chameleon, Squirrel, Cornell, Texas, Wisconsin, and Actor. To rule out data leakage they also test on filtered versions of Chameleon and Squirrel that remove duplicate nodes, and to test scalability they run mini-batch experiments on three large graphs, questions, amazon-ratings, and genius, with hundreds of thousands of nodes.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.necessary: On node classification CoCN attains the best average rank of 1.83 over six datasets, topping Chameleon (79.17%), Squirrel (72.95%) and Cornell (86.22%); on graph classification it wins five of six datasets, including COLLAB (86.15%), IMDB-MULTI (56.32%) and NCI1 (82.89%).
sections.additional: On the filtered Chameleon and Squirrel datasets CoCN ranks first among 18 models (79.61% / 73.27%), showing it is far less sensitive to node-duplicate leakage than the baselines.
sections.audio_script: The results are strong across the board. On node classification, CoCN achieves the best average rank, one point eight three, across the six benchmarks, and it sets the top score on Chameleon at seventy-nine point two percent, Squirrel at seventy-three percent, and Cornell at eighty-six point two percent. On graph classification, it wins five of the six datasets, including COLLAB at eighty-six point one five percent and IMDB-Multi at fifty-six point three percent, and it is competitive on the sixth. On the cleaned, filtered versions of Chameleon and Squirrel, where duplicate nodes are removed, CoCN ranks first out of eighteen models, showing that its advantage is not an artifact of data leakage.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.necessary: Increasing the number of learnable permutations steadily improves accuracy on MUTAG, Chameleon, Cornell and Wisconsin, and enlarging the diagonal-convolution kernel size and receptive field further boosts performance without degradation.
sections.additional: A graph-reconstruction test with an autoencoder shows the relaxed permutations cause almost no information loss even at moderate relaxation factors, confirming the regularization is nearly lossless.
sections.audio_script: Several ablations dissect why CoCN works. First, the number of permutation heads matters: as the model is allowed more permutations, accuracy rises consistently on MUTAG, Chameleon, Cornell, and Wisconsin, because different permutations expose the convolution to different node arrangements. Second, kernel size and receptive field: larger diagonal-convolution kernels give a bigger receptive field and better performance, without the degradation you might fear from over-smoothing. Third, an information-loss study trains an autoencoder to reconstruct graphs from the permuted features and finds that the relaxed, approximate permutations preserve almost all the information, so the regularization is essentially lossless.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.necessary: - Node classification average rank **1.83** across six datasets (best among all baselines). - Squirrel **72.95%** accuracy, versus 61.81% for the best prior model LINKX (a +11 point gain). - COLLAB graph classification **86.15%**, the top result on that dataset. - Permutation-modeling complexity cut from **O(n!)** to **O(n²)**.
sections.additional: Filtered Chameleon / Squirrel first place out of 18 models (79.61% / 73.27%).
sections.audio_script: A few numbers capture the impact. CoCN reaches an average rank of one point eight three across six node-classification datasets, the best of any method tested. On Squirrel it scores nearly seventy-three percent accuracy, more than eleven points above the strongest prior model. On the COLLAB graph dataset it reaches eighty-six point one five percent, the top result there. And perhaps most importantly for scalability, learning the permutation reduces the cost of permutation modeling from n factorial, which is intractable, down to n squared.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.necessary: By learning a task-specific, differentiable permutation that lines up all graph nodes in a row, CoCN brings standard CNN-style diagonal convolution and hierarchical pooling to graphs and achieves state-of-the-art node and graph classification.
sections.additional: The permutation is provably convergent and permutation invariant, and its O(n²) cost makes CNN-on-graphs practical at scale.
sections.audio_script: The takeaway is elegant. If you can learn a differentiable permutation that arranges a graph's nodes into a single row, then all the machinery of ordinary image convolution, sliding kernels, pooling, and hierarchical feature learning, becomes available for graphs. CoCN does exactly this, with a permutation that is provably convergent and permutation invariant, and it turns that idea into state-of-the-art results on both node and graph classification. In short, graphs, all in a row, can be convolved just like images.
